outcome: No source found settles the universal statement since 26 January 2024. Three things happened in 2026 that bear on it, all finite: a self-published computational check of every maximal run with closing prime below 10^12 (forum post and GitHub repository, 27 Aug 2026); a computational check below 10^13 with a Zenodo archive, described by its authors as AI-assisted with Claude (forum post and Zenodo record, 1 Oct 2026); and a Lean 4/Mathlib certificate for every all-composite interval inside [2, 10^4], submitted to the Justin Sun Prize (18 to 24 Sep 2026), closed by the prize repository as a partial formalisation. The official Erdős Problems page (#375) was last edited 24 Jan 2026 and still cites only the 2006 bound of 1.9 × 10^10.
problem_asks: One universal claim, with no separate parts. For every run of consecutive integers n+1, ..., n+k (every starting point n and every length k) in which all members are composite, there exist pairwise distinct primes p_1, ..., p_k with p_i dividing n+i for each i; that is, the members admit a system of distinct prime divisors (a distinct-representatives assignment). Quantified over all n and all k. The bullet does not ask for the weaker Grimm form (the product of k consecutive composites has at least k distinct prime factors), which is a standard weakening and is recorded below only as context.

events.what_happened: C. A. Grimm states the conjecture in the American Mathematical Monthly (1969, pp. 1126-1128) and proves restricted cases. The Erdős Problems history page records that Grimm proved the statement for k of order at most log n / log log n. A search summary also reports special cases n!+2, ..., n!+n and all m > n^(n-1); not checked at the primary source.
events.delivers: Restricted cases only: runs of length k of order at most log n / log log n, for every n (per the Erdős Problems history page). The two special families in the search summary are not checked.
events.remains: The full statement for all k and all n.

checked_by.who: Editors and referees of the American Mathematical Monthly
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record for a problem note of this kind; the referee report is not seen
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the note (not opened at the primary source)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the restricted cases it proves; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Erdős and Selfridge, 'Some problems on the prime factors of consecutive integers II', Proceedings of the Washington State University Conference on Number Theory (1971), pp. 13-21. They state a weaker form (the product of k consecutive composites has at least k distinct prime factors when no prime lies in the interval), derive prime-gap consequences from it, and extend Grimm's range to k at most (1+o(1)) log n. They also treat m > n^pi(n) via Hall's theorem. These details come from the Erdős Problems site and search summaries; the PDF could not be read (binary export).
events.delivers: Restricted cases only: runs of length k at most (1+o(1)) log n (per the Erdős Problems history page), and a range of starting points m above n^pi(n) (search summary). The weaker product form and the gap consequences are conditional on the weaker form, not a result on the bullet's statement.
events.remains: The full statement for all k and all n. The weaker product form is not established by this event.
events.doubts: The PDF was not readable, so Theorem 1 and the stated range were taken from the Erdős Problems page and search summaries.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in restricted cases; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: K. Ramachandra, T. N. Shorey and R. Tijdeman, 'On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers' (J. reine angew. Math., 1975, pp. 109-124, per the citation in the formal-conjectures file), with a sequel 'II' in Crelle's Journal 288 (1976), pp. 192-201 (repository record opened; no abstract). Using Gelfond-Baker methods they prove g(n) >> (log n / log log n)^3, where g(n) is the largest k for which distinct prime divisors exist for n+1, ..., n+k. The Erdős Problems history page records this as the conjecture holding for k of order (log n / log log n)^3.
events.delivers: Restricted cases: for each n, runs of length k up to a constant times (log n / log log n)^3 satisfy the conclusion (per the Erdős Problems history page and Laishram-Murty's lower bound on g(n)).
events.remains: Runs longer than about (log n / log log n)^3 for each n, and so the full statement.

checked_by.who: Journal fur die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Crelle's Journal)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record for number theory
checked_by.what_they_did: Published part I (1975) and part II (1976)

events.doubts: Only the bibliographic record of part II was opened; part I's statement was taken from citations in the Erdős Problems page and the formal-conjectures file.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in restricted cases; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Shanta Laishram and T. N. Shorey, 'Grimm's conjecture on consecutive integers', International Journal of Number Theory 2(2) (2006), pp. 207-211, DOI 10.1142/S1793042106000498. The abstract (opened via the IAS repository; full text not available there) says that for positive integers n and k, primes P_1, ..., P_k with P_i dividing n+i exist whenever n+1, ..., n+k are all composite and n <= 1.9 × 10^10, and calls this a numerical verification of Grimm's Conjecture. The Erdős Problems site states it as true for all k >= 1 and all n <= 1.9 × 10^10.
events.delivers: Finite verification: the statement holds for every k >= 1 and every n <= 1.9 × 10^10 (per the abstract and the Erdős Problems page).
events.remains: Every n above 1.9 × 10^10, so the universal statement.

checked_by.who: International Journal of Number Theory (World Scientific); authors T. N. Shorey and Shanta Laishram
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record; the authors are number theorists
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the numerical verification; the forum calls the bound a 'refereed bound'

events.doubts: A 2008 PuzzLes page quotes a message from T. D. Noe (4 Feb 2008) giving the bound as n <= 19236701629, which is slightly larger than 1.9 × 10^10 and does not match the abstract; see disputes.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the range checked; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Shaohua Zhang, 'A Refinement of the Function g(m) on Grimm Conjecture', arXiv:0811.0966, first submitted 6 Nov 2008; latest version v4, 17 Jan 2011. The abstract says the paper refines the function g(x) on Grimm's conjecture and improves a result of Erdős and Selfridge without using Hall's theorem. The PDF was not readable, so the refined bound is not recorded.
events.delivers: An improved estimate for the function g(m) (the largest k for which the conclusion holds for the block after m). Per the abstract it is a refinement of an Erdős-Selfridge estimate, not a settled case of the conjecture.
events.doubts: No journal publication was located; the arXiv record is the only source opened, and only its abstract was readable.
events.direction: Bears on the g-function, not on the conjecture's truth.

events.what_happened: Andrew R. Hands, 'On Graphical Representations of Grimm's Conjecture and Minimal Interval Lengths', honors thesis, University of Texas at Arlington, dated 1 May 2022 (MavMatrix record). Its abstract (truncated when read) states 'It was then shown Grimm's Conjecture holds for all k <= 31' and describes a method relating n and k. The full text was not read.
events.delivers: Per the abstract: the conjecture holds for all runs of length k at most 31. Whether this holds for all n is not stated in the abstract.
events.remains: Runs of length k of 32 or more, so the full statement.
events.doubts: The phrase 'It was then shown' suggests the k <= 31 result is credited to an earlier source; that source is not identified in what was read.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture in the restricted range k <= 31; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Shanta Laishram and M. Ram Murty, 'Grimm's Conjecture and Smooth Numbers', Michigan Mathematical Journal 61 (2012), pp. 151-160, DOI 10.1307/mmj/1331222852. Posted to arXiv:1306.0765 on 4 June 2013 (v1 only). The abstract bounds g(n) through the distribution of smooth numbers: unconditionally g(n) = O(n^alpha) with 0.45 < alpha < 0.46; under standard conjectures on smooth numbers in short intervals, g(n) = O(n^epsilon). The abstract makes no claim about the conjecture itself. The paper notes that the conjecture would imply g(n) > n' - n, where n' is the smallest prime above n.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 4 Jun 2013 only; the journal version (2012) is earlier.
events.delivers: Bounds on g(n), the quantity the conjecture would control, not on the conjecture itself. Unconditional O(n^alpha) with 0.45 < alpha < 0.46; conditional O(n^epsilon).
events.direction: Bears on the g-function; the conjecture is neither proved nor refuted.

events.what_happened: Shaohua Zhang, 'Generalizations of a theorem about the binomial coefficient', arXiv:0901.3691, first submitted 23 Jan 2009; v2 15 Sep 2009. The abstract generalises a binomial-coefficient theorem to arithmetic progressions and gives a slightly stronger result than Langevin's. The comments field names an earlier version titled 'Generalizations of Several Theorems about the Binomial Coefficient and Grimm Conjecture'.
events.delivers: Results for arithmetic progressions: an analogue of the consecutive-integer statement, not the statement itself.
events.remains: The bullet's statement about consecutive composites.
events.direction: Analogue (arithmetic progressions); does not bear on the consecutive-integer statement.

events.what_happened: M. Langevin, 'Facteurs premiers d'entiers en progression arithmetique' (1977). Reported in search summaries: Langevin notes, by personal communication, that Grimm's conjecture cannot be extended to arithmetic progressions without a proviso (example 12, 25, 38, 51, 64, 77, 90 with ratio 13); he also proposed a stronger multiplicative-independence form. The Langevin paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: A counterexample to a naive extension of the statement to arithmetic progressions. It does not affect consecutive integers.
events.doubts: Reported via search summaries and a forum mention only; the example was not checked at source.
events.direction: Counterexample to the progression analogue, not to the bullet's statement.
events.object: Finite example for the progression analogue: the terms 12, 25, 64 and 90 of the progression 12, 25, 38, ..., 90 (common difference 13) have prime supports inside {2, 3, 5}, so they admit no distinct prime divisors (12 x 25 x 64 x 90 has three distinct prime factors). Explicit, not existential. It shows the naive progression version fails, but it is not a family of consecutive composites.

events.what_happened: Paul Erdős and Carl Pomerance, 'An analogue of Grimm's problem of finding distinct prime factors of consecutive integers', Utilitas Mathematica 24 (1983), pp. 45-65. Per a Zentralblatt review (search summary; not opened): the function uses distinct proper divisors d_m with 1 < d_m < m rather than primes, and a liminf bound holds with equality iff there are infinitely many twin primes. The same search summary says the paper rewrites Grimm's conjecture as the assertion p + g(p) >= p' for consecutive primes p, p'.
events.delivers: An analogue with proper divisors in place of primes. Discounted: it answers a changed question, and its twin-prime equivalence concerns the analogue.
events.doubts: Not opened; the review's OCR garbled the exponents, as the search summary notes.
events.direction: Analogue (proper divisors). Does not bear directly on the statement.

events.what_happened: David Urbanik, 'On the Complexity of Atypical Special Points', arXiv:2512.04491, submitted 4 Dec 2025. The arXiv search listing says it resolves a conjecture of Grimm and Monnee, which is a different conjecture about the flux landscape and integral variations of Hodge structure. The abstract was not opened individually.
events.delivers: Nothing for this problem. It concerns a namesake (Thomas W. Grimm and Jeroen Monnee's conjecture in string-theory flux vacua).
events.direction: Not about this problem.

events.what_happened: Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository (Apache-2.0) adds FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/375.lean in the commit 'feat(ErdosProblems): 375 (#1497)' on 18 Jan 2026. The file defines the statement Erdos375Prop. The main theorem erdos_375 is 'answer(sorry) <-> Erdos375Prop', tagged research open. Variants: bounded_gap (a conditional implication to a prime-gap bound; body contains sorry); legendre (conditional on bounded_gap; no sorry in its own body, but it depends on bounded_gap); le_two (k <= 2, fully proved); log (a conditional Ramachandra-type variant; contains sorry). Later commits to 18 Sep 2026 are refactors and standardisations.
events.revisions: Standardise Erdos Problem Theorems (Mar 2026); refactors and dependency bumps (Jul to Sep 2026). The file's status annotations were not seen to change in the commits listed.
events.delivers: A formal statement of the conjecture, a Lean proof of the trivial k <= 2 case, and conditional formal implications, two of which contain sorry. No formal proof of the conjecture.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks; the main theorem is answer(sorry).
events.directly_checkable: The Lean file states the claim; it is a statement, not a certificate.
events.doubts: The file's own sorry occurrences mean the main theorem is not settled in Lean. The repository README (search summary, not opened) says AlphaProof may be used to find misformalisations across the project; that is a project-level plan and is not known to have been applied to this file.
events.direction: Formal statement only; no direction.

events.what_happened: Terence Tao, Erdős Problems forum post #3273 (16 Jan 2026): says the provenance of the claim that the conjecture implies p_{n+1} - p_n < p_n^(1/2 - c) is 'a little murky'. Theorem 1 of Erdős-Selfridge (1971) gives the weaker bound p_{n+1} - p_n << p_n^(1/2) / log^(1/2) p_n, enough asymptotically for Legendre's conjecture. The power saving is attributed to Ramachandra and likely needs a positive-density version of his result. The post makes no new result.
events.delivers: Nothing on the conjecture itself. It corrects the attribution of a consequence (a prime-gap power saving) and records that the 1971 paper states that bound without proof.

checked_by.qualification: Fields Medallist (2006); professional mathematician working in analysis and number theory
checked_by.what_they_did: Commented on the literature and sketched the Erdős-Selfridge Theorem 1 argument; did not assess the conjecture

events.what_happened: 'DesmondWeisenberg', Erdős Problems forum post #8685 (2 Sep 2026): corrects page references (Er72 p.84; Er73 p.136). Using Hall's marriage theorem, the post states the conjecture for a block of composites is equivalent to a subset condition: for every subset S of the block, the prime divisors of the members of S number at least |S|. It says this already appears in the literature and cites nothing.
events.delivers: A reformulation (an equivalence with a Hall-type subset condition, which is Hall's condition applied to the prime-divisor sets). It establishes no instances. The claim that it already appears in the literature is unsourced.
events.direction: None on the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Forum post #8598 by 'thebrockchain' (27 Aug 2026, 05:17) and GitHub repository grimm-conjecture-verification (README: 'Computed 2026-08-26'; MIT licence; 6 commits, dates not visible). The check covers every maximal run of consecutive composites whose closing prime is below 10^12. The post reports 37,607,912,844 prime gaps, a largest gap of k = 539 after p = 738832927927, a smoothness bound B raised to 2048 from 2.5 × 10^11, zero truncations, and no counterexamples. It describes itself as '52.6x' over Laishram-Shorey and says 'This is a verification, not a proof. The conjecture remains open.' The README's own statement of the bound reads 'below 10^12'.
events.revisions: README computation date 2026-08-26 (not a publication date). Repo commit history not visible.
events.delivers: A finite verification: every run of consecutive composites whose closing prime is below 10^12 has a system of distinct prime divisors. Since a sub-run inherits a matching from the maximal run containing it (my reading), this covers every starting point n below 10^12.
events.remains: Every run with closing prime at or above 10^12, so the universal statement.
events.directly_checkable: Public GitHub repository with code, certificates, and a reproduction script (check.sh, per search summary). Not downloaded or run by me.
events.doubts: (a) Owner inconsistency: the repository page shows owner 'TheEslabonGroup' with path TheEslabonGroup/grimm-conjecture-verification, while the account page for 'thebrockchain' (named on the profile as Brock Falfas) shows 0 public repositories. The forum links the thebrockchain URL. Unresolved. (b) No independent reproduction found. (c) Code not read or run. (d) The repository file list includes a CLAUDE.md file; its contents were not read and it is not a statement by the authors about AI.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; no counterexample below 10^12.

events.what_happened: Justin Sun Prize submission JSP-000310 ('Can distinct prime divisors be assigned to the terms of every run of consecutive composite integers?'). A Lean 4 + Mathlib formalisation in the GitHub repository aznikline/jsp-000310-lean, one commit at 18 Sep 2026 15:26:58 UTC, 'JSP-000310: Grimm's conjecture certified for all intervals in [2, 10^4]'. The commit message says it covers all 1228 maximal composite runs in [2, 10^4]; a separate theorem handles length 2 by a gcd argument. PR #1232 (opened 18 Sep 2026, closed 20 Sep by the author as superseded) and PR #2119 (opened 20 Sep, closed 24 Sep 2026 by contributor Federico2014 because a partial Lean formalisation does not meet the requirements). The author states the full conjecture 'remains open' and that the work is 'a finite certification, scope disclosed'. The catalogue entry (problems/catalog-0301-0400.md) shows status Open and 'Lean proof: No', with no solver or formalizer fields.
events.revisions: PR #1232 (18-20 Sep 2026) superseded by PR #2119 (20-24 Sep 2026), which links the pinned external repository. The repository has one commit.
events.delivers: A finite result: the statement for every all-composite interval inside [2, 10^4] (i.e. every n and k with n+k <= 10^4), plus the length-2 case for all n (unconditional, by gcd(m, m+1) = 1). Nothing for intervals beyond 10^4.
events.remains: Every run with an endpoint above 10^4 of length 3 or more, so the universal statement.

events.what_happened: Erdős Problems forum post #9236 by 'yygotm' (1 Oct 2026, 01:48) and Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.23073168, version 1.1.0, published 1 Oct 2026. The Zenodo creator is Hirotaka Shimizu (ORCID 0009-0005-9508-4917); licence MIT; title 'Grimm's conjecture (Erdős problem #375): computational verification for all runs with closing prime below 10^13'. The post reports that every maximal run of consecutive composites with closing prime below 10^13 has a system of distinct prime representatives: 346,065,536,837 runs, 0 failures, 346,065,536,839 primes, and a longest run of k = 673 after n = 7177162611713. It uses a segmented sieve with bipartite matching, a brute-force cross-check on [2, 2 × 10^6), and a deliberately weakened mode that produces failures. It re-checks runs below 10^12 and cites the 10^12 result above. It calls the work 'a finite verification, not a proof'. The Zenodo package contains C source, an independent brute-force checker, per-chunk logs, SHA-256 checksums and reproduction instructions.
events.revisions: Zenodo version 1.1.0 (1 Oct 2026). Earlier versions are not shown on the record page.
events.delivers: A finite verification: every run of consecutive composites whose closing prime is below 10^13 has a system of distinct prime divisors. This extends the 1.9 × 10^10 bound by a factor of about 500. The post itself states that results above 2 × 10^6 rely on a single implementation.
events.remains: Every run with closing prime at or above 10^13, so the universal statement.
events.directly_checkable: Zenodo archive grimm375-1e13.zip (763.6 kB; MD5 1f33e95145f0f03de4f548d2e0112929 per the Zenodo page), with C source, an independent brute-force checker, per-chunk logs, SHA-256 checksums and reproduction instructions. Not downloaded or run by me.
events.doubts: (a) The post admits results above 2 × 10^6 rely on a single implementation. (b) No independent reproduction was found. (c) The forum handle 'yygotm' shows no name, bio or links; the link to the Zenodo creator rests on the post citing the Zenodo record. (d) AI-assisted code, computation and write-up, as disclosed by the authors; the judging pass should weigh this. (e) The Erdős Problems problem page (last edited 24 Jan 2026) does not reflect this check or the 10^12 one. (f) The 1.9 × 10^10 bound is described in the post as 'refereed'.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; no counterexample below 10^13.

disputes.summary: The stated bound for Laishram and Shorey (2006) differs: the abstract and the Erdős page say n <= 1.9 × 10^10; a PuzzLes page quotes T. D. Noe (4 Feb 2008) saying the conjecture is 'true for all n<=19236701629' citing the same paper. Not resolved; the full paper was not readable.

PuzzLes says 'It has also been proved that there are finitely many exceptions to this Conjecture (B32, R.K.Guy)'. No source was found that supports this. The Erdős Problems page lists the problem as open, and the verifications above are finite. Treated as unsupported.

The forum handle yygotm and the Zenodo creator Hirotaka Shimizu are linked only by the forum post's citation of the Zenodo DOI. The 10^12 repository is shown under owner TheEslabonGroup, while the forum links it under thebrockchain, and the thebrockchain account page shows zero public repositories.
'Devin (aznikline)' is credited in PR #2119 as Lean formalisation author; whether Devin is an AI agent, a person, or someone else is not resolved.

A search summary says arXiv 2609.15597 cites OpenAI's long-gaps preprint and that neither is refereed; the abstract page fetched did not show such a citation (the full text was not readable). Neighbouring problem; recorded for completeness.
Hands (2022) says 'It was then shown Grimm's Conjecture holds for all k <= 31', without naming who showed it first. The attribution of the k <= 31 result is open.

summary: As of 11 October 2026 no source found settles Grimm's conjecture (the universal statement). The events since January 2024 are all finite checks of instances, plus one formal statement. (1) A self-published check of every maximal run of consecutive composites with closing prime below 10^12: forum post #8598 (27 Aug 2026), GitHub repository grimm-conjecture-verification, computed 26 Aug 2026. Its sources show no AI disclosure in what I read; the repository file list includes a CLAUDE.md I did not open, which is a lead and not a statement by the authors. The owner shown on GitHub (TheEslabonGroup) does not match the account named in the forum link (thebrockchain, zero public repositories). (2) A check below closing prime 10^13: forum post #9236 by 'yygotm' (1 Oct 2026) and Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.23073168 (v1.1.0, creator Hirotaka Shimizu). It says the code, computation and write-up were 'produced with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic)' and that the post was 'also reviewed with Codex (OpenAI)'. I have not recorded Codex in ai.systems because the stated role is review of the write-up, which the brief treats as checking, but it stays in this summary. (3) A Lean 4/Mathlib certificate for all all-composite intervals in [2, 10^4], in aznikline/jsp-000310-lean (first commit 18 Sep 2026), submitted to the Justin Sun Prize as JSP-000310 and closed by the prize repository on 24 Sep 2026 as a partial formalisation that does not meet the requirements. PR #2119 credits 'Devin (aznikline)' as Lean author; whether Devin is an AI agent is unresolved, and I did not build the project. The Erdős Problems page (#375) was last edited 24 Jan 2026, still cites only the 2006 bound, and shows no reply to the 2026 posts. The pre-window record is: Erdős-Selfridge 1971 (weaker form, k up to (1+o(1)) log n); Ramachandra-Shorey-Tijdeman 1975/76 (k up to order (log n / log log n)^3); Laishram-Shorey 2006 (n up to 1.9 × 10^10); Hands 2022 thesis (k up to 31, abstract only); and several bounds on the auxiliary function g(n) (Zhang 2008, Laishram-Murty 2012). Those are restricted cases or bounds on g, not settlements. Discounted items: the 1983 Erdős-Pomerance analogue (proper divisors); the arithmetic-progression analogues (Langevin 1977, Zhang 2009), with Langevin's counterexample for progressions; the Grimm-Monnee namesake (arXiv 2512.04491). The neighbouring prime-gap papers (OpenAI 'Improved Long Gaps Between Primes', 3 Sep 2026, attributed to 'GPT-6 Astra' by a tracker, PDF unread; Freiberg arXiv 2609.15597, which credits 'Claude Fable 5.1' for a result on the divisor function of n!) do not mention Grimm. Close calls: (a) Whether the 2026 finite checks count as movement at all. Per §2.1 they check finitely many instances of a universal claim and move no quantity the statement names, which is the Collatz case. On the other reading, the 10^13 check is 500 times the previously published bound, it is the largest verified range in the record, and it is the one event that moves a verified range; a reader could count it as a bound moved. (b) Whether JSP-000310 involves AI: it depends entirely on who or what 'Devin' is. (c) Whether the 10^12 and 10^13 checks come from one author: the handle, the GitHub owner and the Zenodo creator are not tied together by any source I could open beyond the citation in the forum post. Things I checked and did not find: a Grimm result in the Aletheia Gemini run (arXiv 2601.22401; the readable text does not mention 375, appendix unread); any Tao blog post on this problem; an entry for 375 on Tao's AI-contributions wiki (the wiki covers 374 and 380 but not 375); any Grimm result attributed to AlphaProof, Gemini Deep Think, Aristotle, GPT-5.5/5.6 or Astra; any Justin Sun Prize round naming 375 (the 5 Oct 2026 round names #650, #369, #457, #469, #1044 and #1196).
competing_reading: The strongest reading of the 2026 events as progress: the 10^13 check is a named, archived computation (DOI, MIT licence, C source and an independent brute-force checker) covering about 500 times the previously published range; the 10^12 check is independent of it; and a kernel-checked Lean certificate exists for [2, 10^4]. On that reading the problem's verified range moved in 2026, and one event of that kind is AI-assisted (Claude, Anthropic, by the authors' own statement). The opposing reading, which the brief's own examples support (§2.1, Collatz): finitely many instances of a universal claim move nothing the statement names, so none of these is a settlement, and none is even a restricted-case result in the sense of a range of dimensions or a class of objects. The judging pass should weigh both; I have not decided between them.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The identity of 'Devin (aznikline)' in PR #2119: the author's own statement, or the catalogue's solver and formalizer fields for JSP-000310 (not shown in the entry I read). (2) An independent rerun of the 10^13 computation from the Zenodo archive, and a statement from the Zenodo creator or the forum author linking the handle to the record. (3) Ownership history of the thebrockchain repository, to settle whether TheEslabonGroup is the same person or group. (4) An expert or the Erdős Problems maintainer saying whether finite verifications are counted in the problem's status; the page has not changed since January 2026. (5) The full text of Laishram and Shorey (2006), to settle the bound (1.9 × 10^10 or 19236701629); of Hands (2022), to see whether k <= 31 covers all n and who first showed it; and of Erdős-Selfridge (1971), to check Theorem 1. (6) A Lean build of aznikline/jsp-000310-lean with verify.sh, to check the sorry-free claim.

judgement.why: Every post-snapshot event touching the statement is a finite check (10^12, 10^13, Lean certificate on [2,10^4]) and so is instances under F5, however large the range; the competing reading that the verified range is a 'bound' is rejected because the statement names no quantity that a finite search moves. The formal-conjectures file, Tao's attribution note and the Hall reformulation settle nothing (none). The prime-gap preprint, Freiberg's divisor-function paper and the Grimm-Monnee namesake are different questions (variant). Pre-snapshot, Grimm 1969, Erdős-Selfridge 1971, RST 1975 and Hands 2022 settle ranges of k (case); none resolves the whole statement. Laishram-Murty's upper bounds on g(n) do not move the conjecture toward proof or disproof, so none. JSP-000310's 'Devin' quote is bare attribution with no stated mathematical contribution, so none; the 10^13 check discloses Claude produced the code and computation, coded assisted, though the event is discarded as instances.
judgement.doubts: Whether 'Devin (aznikline)' is an AI agent is unresolved; it would not change anything since the event is instances. Freiberg's AI quote is a paraphrase. The Erdős-Selfridge 1971 and Hands ranges were not read at source.
